Yet their rushed development has outpaced critical oversight, leaving key workflow decisions dangerously unscrutinized. We present a much-needed systematic analysis of open-source AI scientist systems, investigating four primary pitfalls: inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post hoc selection bias. Through controlled experiments that isolate each pitfall, we find systematic vulnerabilities across two representative open-source systems. Crucially, we find that these flaws are largely invisible at the level of the final manuscript, suggesting that current manuscript-centric peer review paradigms are fundamentally insufficient for ensuring the integrity of automated research. We further propose mitigation strategies and demonstrate that access to full workflow artifacts (log traces and code) enables more effective auditing. Our findings suggest that journals, conferences, and researchers should move beyond manuscript-only evaluation toward process auditing the end-to-end workflow artifacts of AI scientist systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.1073/pnas.2610214123\", \"pmid\": \"42832657\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13663820\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2610214123\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Closing the Empirical Loop: Autonomous AI Agents Conduct End-to-end Research With Human…

Our findings suggest that journals, conferences, and researchers should move beyond manuscript-only evaluation toward process auditing the end-to-end workflow artifacts of AI scientist systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.1073/pnas.2610214123\", \"pmid\": \"42832657\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13663820\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2610214123\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Closing the Empirical Loop: Autonomous AI Agents Conduct End-to-end Research With Human Participants.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence systems are transforming scientific discovery by accelerating specific research tasks, from protein structure prediction to materials design, yet remain confined to narrow domains requiring substantial human oversight. Exponential growth of scientific literature and increasing domain specialization constrain researchers' capacity to synthesize knowledge across disciplines and develop unifying theories, motivating exploration of general-purpose AI systems for science. Here we show that a domain-agnostic, agentic AI Scientist system can independently navigate the scientific workflow -from hypothesis generation through data collection to manuscript preparation. The system autonomously designed and executed three psychological studies on visual working memory, mental rotation, and imagery vividness, executed online data collection with 288 participants, developed analysis pipelines through 8h+ continuous coding sessions, and produced completed manuscripts. The results demonstrate the capability of AI scientific discovery pipelines to conduct research with theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers, though with limitations in conceptual nuance and theoretical interpretation. This is a step toward embodied AI that can test hypotheses through real-world experiments, accelerating discovery by autonomously exploring regions of scientific space that human cognitive and resource constraints might otherwise leave unexplored. It raises important questions about the nature of scientific understanding and attribution of scientific credit.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.76675\", \"pmid\": \"42734488\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13573717\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76675\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"The New Gravity: How Generative AI Remapped Innovation and What Academia Must Do Next.\", \"abstract\": \"

Unlabelled

Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping clinical research, diagnostics, health system operations, and medical education. Frontier generative AI development is increasingly concentrated in private industry, whose computational infrastructure, proprietary datasets, and capital exceed those of most academic institutions. Although not designed exclusively for medicine, these systems increasingly influence clinical applications. This shift raises a question for academic medical centers (AMCs): What role remains when leading AI systems emerge outside universities? This viewpoint examines industry's growing role in generative AI, clarifies AMCs' responsibilities, and proposes a framework for AI governance and literacy across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education (CME). Rather than compete with industry on computational scale, AMCs should reinforce functions for which AMCs have distinctive strengths. These include (1) mechanistic inquiry linking algorithmic outputs to biological and pathophysiologic understanding; (2) interdisciplinary synthesis integrating clinical, ethical, legal, and sociotechnical perspectives; (3) independent and methodologically rigorous validation of clinical AI tools; and (4) institutional stewardship of ethical governance for patient populations that are often underrepresented in commercial datasets. As nonprofit institutions training clinicians, AMCs have a distinct role in safeguarding transparency, fairness, and accountability in AI-enabled health care. We position this 4-role framework to refine AI governance and translational medicine approaches, clarifying which responsibilities AMCs should retain while collaborating with industry. The approach includes longitudinal AI literacy training across undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, and CME, standardized pathways for evaluating clinical AI, stronger conflict-of-interest safeguards, and complementary partnerships with industry and regulators. We also outline educational assessment methods and safety-monitoring processes, including competency-based assessment across undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, and CME, postdeployment monitoring, and clear escalation triggers. Embedding verification habits and governance into training and practice can help ensure that generative AI supports clinical reasoning while preserving trust, equity, and scientific rigor. This viewpoint addresses academic leaders, curriculum committees, residency directors, faculty developers, and accreditors. Safe clinical AI requires sustained academic leadership.\", \"doi\": \"10.2196/89741\", \"pmid\": \"42896100\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13679860\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.2196/89741\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Conceptual Understanding and Conceptual Change Through Human AI Collaboration in Science Education: An Integrated Conceptual Framework from a Systematic Literature Review.\", \"abstract\": \"Human Artificial Intelligence (Human AI) Collaboration in science education is gaining momentum and more research is required on how it can facilitate students' conceptual understanding and conceptual change. Currently, most studies on AI in science education investigate the use of one particular tool and its effects on learning. However, it is the learning mechanisms that are triggered by these tools that help develop knowledge. This systematic literature review was conducted by performing a systematic search within the Scopus database which was last updated on 15 June 2026. In line with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a total of 28 empirical studies research were analyzed. These studies of empirical research were published between 2023 and 2026. Six roles of AI supporting the students' conceptual understanding as well as five mechanisms supporting the students' conceptual change were identified. Five interconnected learning mechanisms were derived from the analyzed studies, which are presented in an integrated conceptual framework. The framework is based on the theoretical framework of constructivism, the views on learning of the sociocultural theory, the approach of inquiry based science learning as well as on the metacognitive theory. Within the framework AI functions as a learning partner. The framework illustrates how, within science learning environments that are supported by AI, students continuously construct, evaluate and refine their scientific knowledge in order to achieve deeper understanding.\", \"doi\": \"10.12688/f1000research.186991.1\", \"pmid\": \"42800973\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13612998\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.186991.1\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13612998\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13612998?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "c230850920418772f3472e4aa93bb12322e131605207a9fef71039b54d812cf9", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1073/pnas.2610214123", "doi:10.1002/advs.76675", "doi:10.2196/89741", "doi:10.12688/f1000research.186991.1", "pmc:PMC13663820", "pmc:PMC13573717", "pmc:PMC13679860", "pmc:PMC13612998"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2610214123", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13663820?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76675", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.2196/89741", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
